## Where we are

In the first two parts we set up version control and literate programming. Both
are useful by themselves, but they also happen to be the two things you need
before blind analysis is possible at all.

That is what this part is about.

## The problem: researcher degrees of freedom

Between a raw data file and a p-value there are a lot of choices to make:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- which cases to exclude
- how to treat outliers
- which covariates to adjust for
- how to code a variable
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- which model to fit
- what counts as a failed attention check
- what to do about a strange site
- when to stop checking things
:::
:::

Every one of these is defensible. The trouble is that we usually make them after
we can already see which way each one pushes the result.

## This is not mainly about fraud

You do not need bad intentions for this to bite. It is enough to look a bit
harder for problems in the data when the result disagrees with what you
expected, and a bit less hard when it agrees.

That asymmetry is very difficult to notice from the inside, and as far as I know
nobody is immune to it.

## Why the usual fixes don't fully solve it

Preregistration fixes the analysis plan before the data exist. That helps, but
you cannot preregister decisions about data quality problems you have not seen
yet — and those are often the consequential ones.

Reproducibility lets someone re-run your code and get your number back. If the
number was biased, they will reproduce the bias faithfully.

Neither one lets you look at your actual data and still keep the decisions
honest.

## Blind analysis

The idea comes from particle physics, where it has been standard since the
1980s: analyse the data with the answer hidden, finalise every decision, and
only then unblind.

The payoff is that you can inspect your real data and fix its real problems
while the quantity you might be tempted to optimise towards is not visible.

Unblinding happens once, at the end, and you report what comes out.

## It is a protocol, not a lock

Blinding is not encryption. It works the way not opening the randomisation
envelope works — because people agree to follow it.

Today you will have the unblinded data sitting on your laptop, and the exercise
depends on you simply not looking at it. That is also how it goes in a
real lab. The tooling only has to make the honest path convenient.

## What vazul does

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Masking

`mask_labels()`, `mask_variables()`, `mask_names()`

Values are replaced by anonymous labels. Hides what a category means.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Scrambling

`scramble_values()`, `scramble_variables()`

Values are kept but reordered. Breaks the link between columns.
:::
:::

Most protocols end up using both. The name, incidentally, comes from Vazul, an
11th-century Hungarian prince who was blinded to make him ineligible for the
throne.

## Which side do you blind? {.smaller}

Blinding works by breaking the link between predictor and outcome, and a link has
two ends. Scrambling the predictors and scrambling the outcome both do the job,
so the question is really which side you still need intact.

- **Scramble the predictors** when the outcome has to stay usable on its own:
  scale reliability, factor structure, the shape of the outcome distribution.
- **Scramble the outcome** when the predictors have to stay intact — to check
  whether randomisation actually balanced the groups, because the design
  structure is carried by those columns, or simply because there are many
  predictors and only one outcome.

In experiments there is often a third option: mask the condition labels instead.
You can still see that the groups differ, you just cannot tell which group is
which — and not knowing the direction is usually enough.

One thing not to do by accident: scramble both sides independently. That breaks
the link twice over and throws away more than you meant to.

## Grouped scrambling

If the data are clustered — participants in countries, patients in clinics — it
matters a great deal whether you scramble across the whole dataset or within
each cluster.

Scrambling globally hides your effect, but it also flattens the differences
between clusters. That means you lose the ability to notice a site that used a
mistranslated questionnaire, a sample that isn't what you assumed, or a clinic
that entered a scale backwards.

Those are exactly the problems blind analysis is supposed to help you find, so
this argument is worth getting right.

## What each operation preserves {.smaller}

| | distributions | *r* within block | *r* with other columns | cluster means |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| mask | ✅ | — | ✅ | ✅ |
| scramble | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| `.together` | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| `.groups` | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| both | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |

*block* = the columns in one `scramble_variables()` call ·
*cluster* = the grouping named in `.groups`

✅ preserved · ❌ destroyed · masking changes only the category names

The last row is what a confirmatory blinding usually wants.

# The task

## Structure of the task

You will work in pairs. Each of you blinds the MARP data and sends the blinded
file to your partner through a pull request. Then each of you analyses the file
your partner sent, without knowing their seed or their choices.

Everyone does both jobs at the same time, so nobody is waiting on a role.

## One hypothesis

> H1. People who are more religious report higher well-being.

MARP: 10,535 participants across 24 countries.

Your blinded estimate will come out at zero, because scrambling removes the
association entirely. That is expected and not a sign that something broke.

The point of fitting the model blind is to commit to a pipeline — exclusions,
covariates, model form, how you handle anything odd — at a moment when those
choices cannot be bent toward a preferred answer.

## What you are actually practising

At some point in the analysis you will find something in the data that needs a
judgment call.

You will have to write down what you decided, and why, before you unblind. That
is the part worth practising; the rest is scaffolding to get you there.

## Getting started

`exercises/03_blinding/03b_task_brief.qmd`

- find a partner, swap GitHub usernames
- repository up in about five minutes
- blinded and checked by :20
- pull requests exchanged by :30
- analysis and unblinding after that

I will be walking around. Ask early rather than late.

# Debrief

## Questions

1. What did you flag in the data, and what did you decide to do about it?
2. Did unblinding make you wish you had decided differently?
3. Did anything about your partner's blinding limit what you could check?
4. What would you need in order to do this with your own data?

## A detail we skipped past

Before you saw the data, `00_preprocess.R` dropped `gdp`, `ethnicity` and
`denomination`.

`gdp` is constant within a country, so a masked country with a GDP of 57,305 is
identifiable in about ten seconds. `ethnicity` includes values like "Turkish".

A mask is only as good as the columns left sitting next to it, and this is a
common way real blinding protocols leak.

## Doing this properly

One piece we left out: showing that you did not quietly edit the analysis after
unblinding.

The usual approach is to put the analysis in a single Quarto document with a
parameter controlling which data file it reads. Render blinded, commit. Then
unblind, render again, commit. The diff between those two commits is one line,
and that is evidence a reader can check rather than take on trust.
